paragraphs.context: When I write a Magic Tree House book, I draw from three sources
paragraphs.mainIdea: Where the writer gets her ideas, and why writing should be fun.
paragraphs.simple: The writer gets ideas from three places: her imagination, her research and her own life. Her two nephews, Andrew and Peter, are in this story. She says writing should be fun, even when you must write a book many times. She hopes readers will write their own stories.

background.note: A big city on the west coast of the United States, in California, next to the sea.
On April 18, 1906, a very strong earthquake hit San Francisco. Fires then burned most of the city for three days.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie found a magic tree house full of books. It takes them to the places in the books. It belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian. Now they must find four special kinds of writing to help save Camelot. They already have three.

background.note: In old stories about King Arthur, Morgan le Fay is a woman who can do magic. In these books she is a kind librarian.
The castle and city of King Arthur in old British stories.
A king of Britain in very old stories. He and his knights sat at a famous Round Table.

paragraphs.context: Morgan’s note had said, “Come back tomorrow, in the early morning.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why Jack is up so early.
paragraphs.simple: Yesterday Morgan left a note. It told them to come back early this morning.

paragraphs.context: He put on his jeans and T-shirt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack gets ready and goes out quietly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack dresses fast, takes his backpack and goes quietly into the hall, so nobody wakes up.

paragraphs.context: I was waiting for the birds to start singing
paragraphs.simple: Annie is sitting on the steps outside. She was waiting for the birds to sing. Then she was going to wake Jack.

paragraphs.context: Without another word, Jack and Annie left their porch.
paragraphs.simple: They do not talk. They walk up the street to the woods where the tree house is.

paragraphs.context: It was cool beneath the trees.
paragraphs.simple: It is cool under the trees. They hurry to the rope ladder and climb up to the tree house at the top of the tallest oak.

paragraphs.context: Camelot is in trouble. To save the kingdom
paragraphs.simple: Morgan's note says that Camelot is in trouble. To save it, she needs four kinds of writing for her library: something to follow, something to send, something to learn and something to lend.

paragraphs.context: Something to lend
paragraphs.simple: This is the fourth kind. "Something to lend" is something that you give to someone for a time, and they give it back later. This is what they must find today.

paragraphs.context: “We have our first special writing: a list from the Civil War.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: What they have found so far.
paragraphs.simple: They already have three special writings: a list from the Civil War (book 21), a letter from the Revolutionary War (book 22) and a poem from a pioneer school (book 23).

background.note: The American Civil War (1861 to 1865) was a war between the northern and southern states of America.

paragraphs.context: How are they going to save Camelot?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not understand the plan.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders how some old writings can save Camelot. Annie does not know, but she wants to start now and find the answer.

paragraphs.context: Their Pennsylvania book, the book that always brought them home
paragraphs.simple: Their Pennsylvania book can always take them home. Next to it is a new book. It is about San Francisco, California, in 1906.

paragraphs.context: I guess I told Miss Neely the truth after all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A joke about the last adventure.
paragraphs.simple: In the last book, Annie told the teacher Miss Neely that they were going to California. She did not really mean it. Now it is true, so she laughs.

background.note: The teacher at the pioneer school in book 23, Twister on Tuesday.

paragraphs.context: The wind started to blow.
paragraphs.simple: The wind blows, and the tree house spins faster and faster. Then everything stops. This means they have arrived in a new place and time.

paragraphs.context: Annie was wearing a blue-and-white dress with a big sailor collar
paragraphs.simple: The magic has given them clothes from 1906. Annie has a dress with a big collar and white stockings. Jack has short trousers, a jacket, a cap and a tie. His backpack is now a leather bag.

paragraphs.context: Painted wooden houses and gaslights lined a quiet cobblestone street.
paragraphs.mainIdea: What they see from the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is at the bottom of a hill. There is a quiet old street with wooden houses, gas lamps and a trolley car. Tall buildings are farther away, and the sun is coming up behind them.

background.note: In 1906, many street lamps burned gas. Electric street lights were still new.
A kind of bus that runs on rails in the street. San Francisco is famous for its cable cars, which are like this.

paragraphs.context: On Wednesday, April 18, 1906, San Francisco was the biggest city
paragraphs.mainIdea: What the research book says about San Francisco.
paragraphs.simple: In 1906 San Francisco was the biggest city on the west coast of America. Half a million people lived there, and it was very beautiful.

paragraphs.context: Jack pulled out his notebook. He wrote:
paragraphs.simple: Jack writes notes, as he always does. (The notes are a picture in the book, so the words are not here.)

paragraphs.context: She took the book and notebook away from him
paragraphs.simple: Annie does not want to wait. She puts Jack's book and notebook in his bag. Jack says research is not a waste of time, but he follows her.

paragraphs.context: Let’s just explore and see the sights. We can be tourists.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to walk around and look at the city, like people on holiday. Jack reminds her that they must find the writing for Morgan.

paragraphs.context: The early light turned everything to gold
paragraphs.simple: The morning sun makes everything look gold. The city is quiet. Everyone seems to be asleep.

paragraphs.context: The noise got louder. It sounded like thunder coming from under the ground.
paragraphs.simple: A deep noise comes from under the ground. Then the earth starts to shake.

paragraphs.context: The whole street began to move.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The street moves like the sea.
paragraphs.simple: The whole street moves. The stones in the road go up and down like waves in the sea.

paragraphs.context: “Get down!” shouted Jack. “Cover your head!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to get down low and cover her head. This is what you should do in an earthquake, because things fall from above.

paragraphs.context: Then the world grew still. The rumbling stopped.
paragraphs.simple: Everything is quiet again. The air is full of dust. They think the earthquake is over.

paragraphs.context: I guess I should have let you do a little more research on this place
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she should have let Jack read more first. Jack agrees, but he says that even with more research, they could not have stopped an earthquake.

paragraphs.context: Then the terrible shaking started. It was even harder than before.
paragraphs.simple: The earthquake comes again, even stronger. Jack is thrown to the ground. Tall buildings move from side to side, roofs fall in, and pieces of buildings fall into the street.

paragraphs.context: A cloud of dust billowed around Jack.
paragraphs.simple: There is so much dust that Jack cannot breathe or see. He hears Annie coughing and calling his name.

paragraphs.context: He hurt all over. His clothes were ripped
paragraphs.simple: Jack hurts everywhere. His clothes are torn and dirty, and his cap is gone. His legs are so weak that he falls down again.

paragraphs.context: “I fell into the ground!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie has fallen into a big crack in the ground. Jack crawls toward her voice and finds her in the crack.

paragraphs.context: Bring me something to stand on
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks for something to stand on. Jack gives her bricks one by one. She puts them on top of each other like steps.

paragraphs.context: He was afraid there’d be another earthquake and the crack would close
paragraphs.simple: Jack is afraid that the ground will shake again and the crack will close with Annie inside. So he works fast.

paragraphs.context: At last, Annie finished stacking the bricks.
paragraphs.simple: Annie stands on the bricks and pulls herself out with her hands. She is dirty, her stockings are torn and her knees are hurt.

paragraphs.context: “A little shaky,” said Jack. Actually, he was very shaky.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is not telling the whole truth.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says he is "a little" shaky, but really he is very shaky. He does not want Annie to worry.
paragraphs.tone: Jack is brave in front of his sister, but very afraid inside.

paragraphs.context: At 5:13 A.M. on April 18, 1906, the people of San Francisco were shaken awake
paragraphs.simple: The earthquake came at 5:13 in the morning, so it woke everyone up. It was one of the biggest earthquakes in American history. People called it "the Great Shake".

background.note: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake was very strong (about 7.9). About 3,000 people died, mostly in the fires after it.

paragraphs.context: families were stumbling out of their crumbling houses
paragraphs.mainIdea: People come out of their houses.
paragraphs.simple: Families come out of their broken houses in their night clothes and with no shoes. Small children cry, but the adults are silent and just stare.

paragraphs.context: “Everyone must be in shock,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the people are in shock: something so bad has happened that they cannot think or feel normally. Jack feels the same. He cannot think clearly.

paragraphs.context: Just after the earthquake, broken chimneys, stoves, and lamps caused terrible fires.
paragraphs.simple: Broken chimneys, stoves and lamps started fires. The fires burned for three days and destroyed most of the city: more than 28,000 buildings.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, a cloud of black smoke was rolling through the sky.
paragraphs.simple: Far away, they see black smoke in the sky. The fires that the book talked about are starting.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe we should leave,” Jack said in a panic.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is very afraid. He wants to leave before the fires spread. Annie says they must stay and find the writing for Morgan.

paragraphs.context: They saw houses leaning to one side and people hauling their things out to the street.
paragraphs.simple: Everywhere there are broken bricks, glass, fallen lamps and twisted trolley tracks. Some houses lean to one side. People carry their things out into the street.

paragraphs.context: He was so shaky, he didn’t think he could be much help to anyone.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to help, but Jack feels weak.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says that helping people is more important than their mission now. Jack feels too weak and afraid to help anyone.

paragraphs.context: We’re trying to get these bank bags down to the harbor
paragraphs.simple: Men are putting bags of money from a bank into a wagon. They will take them to the sea and put them on a boat, so the fires cannot burn the money.

background.note: A place by the sea where ships stay. San Francisco has a big bay and a busy harbor.

paragraphs.context: Jack wished he and Annie could ride with the driver down to the bay
paragraphs.simple: Jack wishes they could go with the driver to the bay, where it is safe. But there is no room in the wagon.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, what’s the story?” a woman asked.
paragraphs.simple: A woman asks them what is happening. Her voice shows that she needs to know fast. She is a newspaper reporter, and the man with her is a photographer.

paragraphs.context: “For television?” asked Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks if Betty works for TV. But in 1906 there was no TV yet, so Betty does not understand. Jack quickly says "Never mind".

background.note: TV was invented in the 1920s, about twenty years after this story.

paragraphs.context: “Good reporting work, sonny!”
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Betty about the bank money. Betty is happy with his answer, and she tells Fred to take a photo of the bank.

paragraphs.context: He put his head under a black curtain and took a picture.
paragraphs.simple: Fred puts his camera on a stand and puts his head under a black cloth to take the photo. Cameras in 1906 were big and slow, and the cloth kept out the light.

paragraphs.context: By the end of three days, the fires will burn down nearly all of San Francisco.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says what the research book said: the fires will burn down most of the city in three days. Betty is surprised that she knows this, so Jack says she is only guessing.

at the same time.example: At the same time, it requires lots of work

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: They are about to set off

beat it.meaning: Go away quickly! (Friendly talk.) "Let's beat it" means let's leave fast.

blow up.meaning: To destroy something with an explosion.
blow up.example: He ordered some buildings to be blown up by dynamite.

bring to a halt.meaning: To stop something, like a car or a wagon.
forms: brought his wagon to a halt
bring to a halt.example: He brought his wagon to a halt.

brush off.meaning: To clean dust or dirt off something with your hand.
brush off.example: As he brushed off his pants

burn down.meaning: To burn until it is completely destroyed. For a building: to be destroyed by fire.
burn down.example: the fires will burn down nearly all of San Francisco.

can't help.meaning: "Couldn't help smiling" means could not stop himself from smiling.

catch one's breath.meaning: To start breathing normally again after running.
catch one's breath.example: said Jack, trying to catch his breath.

cave in.meaning: To fall down into the inside. "Roofs were caving in" means roofs were falling down into the houses.

check out.meaning: To look at something to learn about it.
check out.example: You might want to check out our Readers & Writers Club

come up with.meaning: To think of an idea or a plan.
come up with.example: my imagination came up with the idea of Jack and Annie visiting San Francisco

end up.meaning: To be in a place or a situation at the end, often without planning it.
end up.example: you might end up in the middle of an earthquake!

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: Find out where your imagination, your research, and your own experiences lead you.

for now.meaning: For a short time; until later. "Good-bye for now" means good-bye until we meet again.

from head to toe.example: She was caked with dust from head to toe.

get going.meaning: To start moving or doing something; to leave.
get going.example: But let’s get going so we can solve the mystery.

get out of.example: He wanted to get out of San Francisco before the fires spread.

give up.meaning: To stop trying; to stop hoping.
give up.example: The brave citizens of the city never gave up hope.

go up in flames.example: buildings were going up in flames.

had better.meaning: Should. "We'd better help" means we should help.

hold on to.meaning: To hold something tightly so you do not fall or lose it.
hold on to.example: She was holding on to the rope ladder.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand toward someone to give them something.
hold out.example: Andrew held out the piece of wood to Jack and Annie.

hold up.meaning: To lift something so people can see it.

if at first you don't succeed.meaning: The start of a saying: "If at first you don't succeed, try, try again." It means: if you fail the first time, keep trying.
forms: if at first you don’t succeed
if at first you don't succeed.example: ‘If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again,’

in a panic.meaning: Very afraid, so that you cannot think clearly.

in shock.meaning: Feeling strange, weak and unable to think after something very bad has happened.

in the middle of.meaning: In the centre of a place, or during an event.
in the middle of.example: end up in the middle of an earthquake!

in trouble.meaning: In a bad or dangerous situation.

make up.meaning: To form something; to be the parts of something.
make up.example: the rocky plates that make up the earth’s surface.

never mind.meaning: It is not important; forget it.

no longer.example: they were no longer in the magic tree house.

on hand.meaning: Near you and ready to use.

on one's way.meaning: Going to a place; travelling there now.
on one's way.example: they were on their way to California.

on top of.meaning: On the highest part of something.
on top of.example: Annie carefully stacked the bricks on top of each other.

once again.example: San Francisco was once again one of the loveliest cities

one by one.example: handed them down to Annie, one by one.

out of control.meaning: Too strong for people to stop.
out of control.example: Fires are burning out of control.

pack up.meaning: To put your things into a bag or box before you leave.
pack up.example: As the photographer packed up his equipment

pull apart.meaning: To move away from each other.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place.
put away.example: Just as he put the book away

put on.example: He put on his jeans and T-shirt.

put out.meaning: To make a fire stop burning.
put out.example: After the earthquake fires were put out

read someone's mind.meaning: To know what someone is thinking.

rows and rows.example: Along the walls were rows and rows of tall bookcases

rush off.example: the two of them rushed off.

see the sights.meaning: To visit the famous or interesting places in a town.
see the sights.example: Let’s just explore and see the sights.

set off.meaning: To start a trip. "Setting off dynamite" means making dynamite explode.
set off.example: They are about to set off to find the third of these

set up.meaning: To get a machine ready to use.
set up.example: Fred was setting up his camera.

shaken up.meaning: Upset and afraid after something bad has happened.

shock wave.meaning: A strong wave of movement that goes through the ground (or the air) after an earthquake or explosion.

straighten up.meaning: To sit or stand with your back straight.
straighten up.example: The man straightened up a little.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm.

take a trip.example: I can’t believe we took a trip to Morgan’s library

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.example: I’ll take care of the library.

take notes.meaning: To write down things so that you remember them.

take off.example: Then he and his horses took off.

the way we came.meaning: By the same road that we used to get here.
the way we came.example: I guess we just go back the way we came.

throw on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag quickly.
throw on.example: He threw on his pack and followed Annie.

time and space.example: She travels through time and space, gathering books.

trail off.meaning: For a voice: to get quieter and then stop.

up to.meaning: 1. As many as; not more than. 2. Toward something ("held it up to the window").

wake up.meaning: To stop sleeping; or to make someone stop sleeping.
wake up.example: Then I was going to wake you up.

watch out.meaning: Be careful! (You say it when there may be danger.)
watch out.example: But watch out—you might end up in the middle of an earthquake!

without another word.example: Without another word, Jack and Annie left their porch.

work into.meaning: To put something into a story or a plan.
work into.example: true facts are often worked into the story.
